Home/IoT sensors/Temperature, humidity & light sensor

Temperature, humidity
and light sensor.
Indoor conditions.
Connected to your team.

The Hitelecom H Series temperature, humidity and light sensor measures local air temperature, relative humidity and illuminance for indoor monitoring. Designed for museums, galleries, archives and other managed spaces, it connects conditions at selected points with remote review and configured alerts. Custom sensor configurations can be discussed for additional sensing and installation requirements. Choose H200 LoRa, H300 4G or H500 NB-IoT, then match the sensing layout, light measurement and reporting profile to your project.

KEY FEATURES

Three measurements.
One clear view of the space.

Connect room conditions, collection environments and light exposure with the people responsible for them.

Temperature. Humidity. Light.

Three complementary measurements help teams understand the conditions around collections, stored materials and occupied rooms.

Measure where it matters

Plan positions around display areas, cases, shelving and room zones. Select the sensing arrangement for the conditions you want to observe.

Your monitoring targets

Agree temperature and humidity limits with the people responsible for the space or collection, then configure the alert workflow.

Three wireless choices

H200 LoRa, H300 4G and H500 NB-IoT support different site networks and deployment plans.

Custom sensors for your project

Match the sensing channels, product form and mounting arrangement to your space. Share your requirements for a project-specific configuration.

Remote project visibility

Connect to Hitelecom Platform or an agreed customer platform for measurement review and configured temperature and humidity alerts.

TEMPERATURE · HUMIDITY · LIGHT · CUSTOM SENSING

See the conditions.
Understand the context.

Room averages tell part of the story. Conditions beside an exhibit, within a display case or near stored materials can differ. A useful monitoring plan identifies both the place being measured and the decision each reading will support.

SENSING & INSTALLATION

Choose a representative position.
Keep the light path clear.

Mark each monitoring point on a room or case plan. For air measurements, choose exposure that represents the monitored zone and account for nearby vents, doors and heat sources. For illuminance, keep the sensing face unobstructed and record its orientation. Agree reversible mounting for heritage interiors and collection spaces.

FROM READING TO RESPONSE

From room conditions.
To a considered response.

Build the monitoring profile around the change you want to see. The measurement interval defines when readings are taken; the reporting interval defines when data reaches the platform. Specify both alongside your alert and battery requirements.

01

Define the points

Identify rooms, cases and material zones. Record the purpose and location of each sensing point.

02

Set the profile

Agree measurement and reporting intervals, channel specifications and temperature and humidity alert targets.

03

Review the conditions

Use readings alongside the lighting schedule, room operation and collection-care plan to decide what to investigate or adjust.

CONFIGURATION & OPERATING PROFILEMatched to your site. Agreed for your project.

The published reference configuration is designed for more than 10 years with 10-minute sampling and reporting every four hours. Sampling and reporting intervals can be agreed for the project, and actual service life depends on the battery pack, selected sensor channels, operating temperature and radio conditions. For a temperature, humidity and light installation, confirm the battery plan against the final channel list, reporting profile, operating temperature and network conditions.

See the conditions around the collection, from gallery air to individual cases. Temperature and relative humidity establish the local climate; optional illuminance readings support the exhibition lighting plan.

Museum gallery environments

Temperature and relative humidity; optional illuminance at selected display positions.+

Build an environmental record for each gallery rather than relying on one reading for the whole museum. Compare display zones through opening hours, evening shutdown and seasonal changes. Measurements to monitor
Temperature and relative humidity; optional illuminance at selected display positions.
Measurement point

Placement & installation

ANSWERS FOR YOUR PROJECT

Frequently
asked questions.

Practical answers for choosing measurement points, collection targets and a wireless monitoring configuration.

Ask about your project ↗
What does a temperature, humidity and light sensor measure?+

It measures air temperature, relative humidity and illuminance at selected indoor sensing points. Illuminance is expressed in lux and describes the visible light falling on a surface.

Specify the channels, sensing arrangement and measurement performance for the supplied Hitelecom configuration.

Why monitor temperature, humidity and light together in a museum?+

They describe different parts of the environment around a collection. Temperature and humidity observations support climate review; light observations support decisions about display lighting and exposure schedules.

Reading them in the context of the exhibit, its materials and opening hours gives conservators and facilities teams a shared basis for discussion.

How should we choose temperature, humidity and light targets for collections?+

Start with the collection's materials, their condition, the existing environment and any agreed loan or exhibition requirements. Ask the conservation team to define the targets for each room or case.

Temperature and humidity limits can then inform the alert configuration, while light readings can be compared with the agreed display plan.

Where should sensors be placed in galleries, archives and display cases?+

Place the air-sensing point where it represents the collection or zone you want to monitor. Consider shelving height, nearby walls, vents and doors. Treat an enclosed case as its own monitoring location when its internal conditions are important.

Record the point on the site plan and agree the terminal or probe arrangement before installation.

Where should the light-sensing face be positioned for an exhibit?+

Choose a position and orientation that represent the illuminated surface or display area being assessed. Keep the sensing face clear of shadows from the enclosure, mounts or nearby objects, and record its direction.

Use a commissioning light check at the exhibit to confirm that the fixed monitoring position answers the intended lighting question.

How are lux readings used when reviewing exhibition lighting?+

Compare the measured light level with the exhibit's lighting target and note how it changes with daylight, lamp settings and opening hours. Both intensity and duration matter when planning exposure for light-sensitive materials.

If the project requires cumulative exposure analysis, include time-stamped illuminance data, units and the calculation workflow in the platform brief.

How should measurement and reporting intervals be selected?+

Choose the measurement interval around the changes you need to observe, such as lighting schedules, case access or room operation. Choose the reporting interval around the team's remote-review and alert needs.

Agree both with the required data coverage and battery plan. A project intended to study brief changes needs a different profile from a long-term seasonal overview.

Which wireless model and platform should we choose for an indoor installation?+

Choose H200 for LoRa, H300 for 4G or H500 for NB-IoT. Evaluate coverage at the actual monitoring points, including enclosed cases, basement stores and internal rooms.

For LoRa, plan the gateway and platform path. For cellular models, confirm local network service and provisioning. Hitelecom Platform or an agreed customer platform can form the monitoring destination.

What measurement performance and calibration information should we specify?+

Specify the expected operating conditions and required range, accuracy and resolution for each channel. For light, include the expected low-light or brighter-room conditions and sensing orientation.

Agree how readings will be checked at commissioning, which calibration documents the project needs and a review schedule suited to the installation. Compare the supplied specification with the measurement task.

What should be included when planning battery life?+

Use the selected channel list, measurement and reporting intervals, operating conditions and network quality to define the battery plan. Confirm the calculation for the supplied temperature, humidity and light configuration.

The published T&H reference design states more than 10 years with 10-minute sampling and reporting every four hours under stated test conditions. Sampling and reporting intervals can be agreed for the project, and actual service life depends on the battery pack, selected channels, operating temperature and radio conditions. Match that reference to the final project configuration.
